questions.prompt: Your file-reading code catches `except Exception`. Why is that usually worse than catching `except FileNotFoundError`?
choices: It also swallows the bugs you did not anticipate, and reports them as a missing file
Exception is not a real class
You can only use Exception once in a program
questions.explain: A broad except hides the errors you have not thought of yet, behind a message that is now untrue.

questions.prompt: Which of these are edge cases for a task manager?
choices: Viewing the list when there are no tasks
A task name that is an empty string
Marking a task number larger than the list
questions.explain: Adding one ordinary task is the normal case, and worth testing too, but it is not an edge. Edges are the empty, the oversized and the missing.

questions.prompt:
___:
    n = int(input("Number: "))
___ ValueError:
    print("Please type a number.")
questions.explain: The try holds the code that might fail; the except names the one failure you are ready for and says what to do about it.

questions.prompt: Which of these tests would still pass if add_task were replaced by a function that does nothing?
choices: Checking the list holds one task after adding one
Checking the added task has the name you passed in
Checking the call returns the list
questions.explain: A test that only checks a function is there passes against any function at all, including one that does nothing. A test earns its place by failing when the behaviour is wrong.

questions.prompt: Your program crashed. Put the steps in the order that finds the cause.
items: Read the error and the line it names
Reproduce it on purpose with the input that caused it
Run that case again, and the ones that already passed
questions.explain: Re-running the cases that already passed is the step people skip, and it is the one that catches a fix that broke something else.
